title: Indra Sawhney v. Union of India
outcome: Caste can be a relevant indicator of social and educational backwardness. Reservations under Article 16(4) were upheld for Other Backward Classes, subject to a 50% ceiling in ordinary circumstances, exclusion of the creamy layer, and no reservation in promotions (as then held).
ratio: Article 16(4) is a facet of equality, not an exception that destroys equality of opportunity.
Caste may be used as a starting point for identifying backward classes, but the class must be both socially and educationally backward.
The creamy layer of socially advanced persons must be excluded from OBC reservation.
Reservations should not exceed 50% except in extraordinary situations.
As held in 1992, Article 16(4) did not permit reservation in promotions (later modified by constitutional amendment and subsequent cases).

key_holdings.holding: OBC reservation upheld with creamy-layer exclusion

overruled_or_modified: The bar on reservation in promotions was later addressed by the 77th, 81st, 82nd and 85th Amendments and cases such as M. Nagaraj (2006) and Jarnail Singh (2018); verify current promotion-reservation law separately
followed_by: M. Nagaraj v. Union of India (2006)
Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India (2022) (EWS)
summary: Indra Sawhney is the principal authority on OBC reservation, creamy layer, and the 50% ceiling. Later amendments changed the promotions question; the identification and creamy-layer holdings remain central.
content_for_rag:
Indra Sawhney v. Union of India 1992 Supp (3) SCC 217; AIR 1993 SC 477, decided on 16 November 1992 by a nine-judge bench, is the Mandal Commission case. It examined the validity of reservations for Other Backward Classes in Central Government employment under Article 16(4).

The Court held that caste can be a relevant indicator of social and educational backwardness, but the beneficiary class must actually be backward. The creamy layer — the socially advanced among a backward class — must be excluded. Reservations should ordinarily not exceed 50%, save extraordinary situations. Article 16(4) was read as a facet of equality of opportunity, not a rival to Article 16(1).

The 1992 holding that Article 16(4) did not permit reservation in promotions was later overtaken by constitutional amendments and a distinct line of cases (Nagaraj, Jarnail Singh). For current advice, separate the still-binding identification/creamy-layer/50% discussion from the later promotions and EWS jurisprudence. This seed note is not a complete gazette of reservation law.
